rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God placed a divine spark in each person that enables discernment between good and evil.
rows.anchor: It is this divine spark which enables a person to discern good from evil.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because people can distinguish good from evil, they must choose good and shun evil; this brings success, while vice leads to misery.
rows.anchor: When a person has been given the awareness of good and evil, then it is his obligation to adopt good and shun evil.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form dassāhā derives from a root meaning to wrap or put something in dirt, with a transformation intensifying the sense of contamination.
rows.anchor: the root which means “to wrap up something in dirt and to put something into dirt.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Using every divine favour rightly serves one’s own interest and expresses gratitude; failing to do so is self-destruction.
rows.anchor: every favour God has bestowed on him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As a person who closes his eyes risks falling and bears responsibility, a person must stay alert to the moral path he follows.
rows.anchor: there is a strong probability that he might fall in a pit and he himself would be responsible for this mishap and no other person.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take 91:9–10 as the oath’s complement; Islahi gives weight to al-Zamakhsharī’s rejection of that view.
rows.anchor: there is weight in his rejection.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun, moon, day, and night show that a powerful, self-sustaining God keeps the world’s elements on their appointed paths, preventing their collision from destroying it.
rows.anchor: The oaths which are sworn here by the sun, the moon, the day and the night are referring to the fact that the reins of all elements

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oaths by sky and earth point to the Creator’s power, wisdom, and providence, implying that no one escapes accountability for deeds.
rows.anchor: the oaths sworn by the sky and the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath by the human soul makes its own nature evidence: God’s inborn awareness of good and evil entails success for good and a dreadful fate for evil.
rows.anchor: The third oath is sworn by the way human soul has been formed which occupies the status of evidence borne by man’s inner self.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The purification and corruption statement explains one aspect of the final oath rather than serving as its complement; Islahi endorses al-Zamakhsharī’s view that the complement is suppressed.
rows.anchor: a suppression of the muqsam ‘alayh has occurred here.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Suppressing the complement lets everything evident from the oaths count as its content; one prominent implication is that God destroys rebellious nations.
rows.anchor: The benefit of this suppression is that everything

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nations are punished collectively in this world for collective rebellion, while each person is individually judged and rewarded or punished in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: In the Hereafter, each person will be held accountable in his personal capacity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Historical evidence shows that a rebellious nation is given time and a clear warning, then destroyed if it persists in denial without excuse.
rows.anchor: it is communicated the truth to the extent that it is left with no excuse to deny the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cosmic and inward evidence mainly serves reflective intellectuals; historical incidents can move ordinary people who are able to learn from them, so the Qur’an uses both forms of proof.
rows.anchor: evidence from incidents and events are more effective

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an mentions Thamūd alone here, although it names many nations elsewhere; its history was especially familiar to the Quraysh.
rows.anchor: has mentioned many nations to highlight this aspect

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi quotes his mentor Imām Farāhī: Quraysh knew the Thamūd’s history, and the Qur’anic allusion was enough to evoke the whole account, including their inherited settlements and traditions.
rows.anchor: has discussed their history and their resemblance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brief Qur’anic account could evoke the Thamūd’s full fate for the Quraysh because their history was familiar and often discussed among them.
rows.anchor: was enough to point to their complete history

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited Arabic couplet treats Qidār as a figure overcome by time, evidence that Thamūd were known in Arab poetry.
rows.anchor: The poets have also mentioned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qidār, who killed the she-camel, was an autocratic and rebellious Thamūd leader, comparable to Qayl ibn ʿUmar of ʿĀd.
rows.anchor: He was an autocratic and rebellious leader

rows.speaker: al-Afwah al-Awdī
rows.claim: Al-Afwah compares his nation’s corrupt elements to Qayl and Qidār, portraying them as destructive, resistant to guidance, and driven by folly and rebellion.
rows.anchor: The famous poet al-Afwah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thamūd’s rebellion, leaders’ deviance, and fate were proverbial among Arabs, so the Qur’an’s short reference conveyed a full history to its first audience.
rows.anchor: so well known to the Arabs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭaghwā means insurgency against God’s bounds, especially rebellion after truth has become clear.
rows.anchor: It means insurgency and rebelling against the bounds and limits set by the Almighty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word connects the passage to its central theme: Thamūd denied their prophet from arrogance after truth was evident, not because it was unclear.
rows.anchor: they in fact denied him after the truth had become obvious to them merely out of their arrogance and rebelliousness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qidār’s callousness led the nation toward destruction; the verb describing his rising means preparing for the crime that opened God’s wrath.
rows.anchor: which opened the doors of God’s wrath on the whole nation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Ṣāliḥ warned them, Thamūd demanded a sign; he made the she-camel both a sign of punishment and a test with an assigned drinking turn.
rows.anchor: nominated a she-camel as a sign for this punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Thamūd hamstrung the camel, God gave them three days to repent; the respite increased their arrogance, and punishment destroyed them.
rows.anchor: After this, the Almighty granted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣāliḥ’s words describe his final warning to Thamūd to honor God’s she-camel and her turn to drink or face punishment.
rows.anchor: resolved to destroy the wall

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative phrase about God’s she-camel uses tahdhīr, with an omitted warning verb that focuses the listener; the warning style is common across languages.
rows.anchor: in the accusative on account of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thamūd ignored this last warning just as they had rejected the earlier threat, dismissing it as intimidation and pressure.
rows.anchor: mere intimidation and a pressure tactic

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAqr literally means hamstringing a camel; since that causes certain death, killing is an implied, resultant sense rather than the primary meaning.
rows.anchor: to hamstring a camel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although one person killed the camel, God attributes the crime and punishment to the whole nation because it sanctioned the act; only those who tried to reform him or dissociated themselves were spared.
rows.anchor: one person was responsible for killing the she-camel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Damdamah denotes killing with great intensity; Islahi renders it a resounding punishment and connects it to the scourge described elsewhere.
rows.anchor: very appropriate for such a punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The severe punishment fits the camel’s role as a sign and trial of the nation’s rebellion; God punished them for harming it despite warnings.
rows.anchor: punishment was meted out to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The camel tested the whole nation’s rebellion; further respite might have led them to kill the Messenger, a crime that always brings a nation’s destruction.
rows.anchor: whenever a nation planned to kill its Messenger, it was necessarily destroyed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi suggests the sūrah came while Quraysh leaders secretly plotted Muhammad’s killing at Dār al-Nadwah; it alludes to consequences and urges reflection.
rows.anchor: conspire in their gatherings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fasawwāhā means God’s scourge flattened them; its feminine pronoun can refer either to Thamūd or to their settlements.
rows.anchor: the scourge and punishment of the Almighty absolutely flattened and steamrolled them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When God destroys a nation, He acts by a practice grounded in full knowledge and power for the world’s welfare, with no fear of error, challenge, or accountability.
rows.anchor: nor does He have any fear

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse refutes interpolated Torah depictions of God regretting creation and promising after Noah not to punish again because human evil persists.
rows.anchor: This verse also refutes the statements of the Torah which its narrators have inserted into it.

none: Closing gratitude, completion notice, and date only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah al-Layl pairs with al-Shams; their central themes and inner and outer features correspond so closely that even a general reader can sense the harmony.
rows.anchor: There is no essential difference between the central themes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Layl develops the preceding sūrah’s claim that the soul succeeds through purification by identifying what corrupts it and how it can be protected and purified.
rows.anchor: the things which contaminate it are explained

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–4 use evidence from the outer and inner worlds to establish that Judgment must come: the Hereafter is this world’s counterpart and makes it meaningful.
rows.anchor: The evidence of the world around man and the world within him is presented to show that the Day of Judgement is bound to come.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 5–7 describe the character and belief that qualify a person for success in the Hereafter and ease the way to it.
rows.anchor: Mentioned in these verses are the character and ideology which entitles a person to the successes of the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 8–10 describe the character and belief that lead a person to doom and Hell.
rows.anchor: Mentioned in these verses are the character and ideology of a person which lead him to doom and to the pit of Hell.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 11–14 admonish Quraysh that God guides through revelation but does not force acceptance; they alone benefit from accepting, while both worlds remain under His control.
rows.anchor: this world and the next are in the grasp of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 15–21 explain the traits of those cast into Hell and those shielded from it, together with their reward.
rows.anchor: An explanation of the character of people who will be thrown into Hell and those who will be shielded from it

none: Only the final words completing the preceding outline sentence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Oaths by natural phenomena in the Qur’an are intended to establish a premise.
rows.anchor: the various oaths sworn by natural phenomena are meant to substantiate a

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night and day, like male and female, are complementary pairs whose members fill one another’s void and together serve their created purpose; without a counterpart, their capacities and uses make no sense.
rows.anchor: the male and female species form complementary pairs and together these pairs fulfil the purpose for which they have been created

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The harmony of opposites argues for monotheism and, here, for the Hereafter; 51:49 calls pairs a reminder that this world has a counterpart completing its purpose.
rows.anchor: argument to substantiate the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In verse 3, mā makes the verb a verbal noun; Islahi says he already explained this grammatical point under 91:5.
rows.anchor: converts a verb into a verbal noun

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The paired order of creation proves this world has an afterlife counterpart; without it, life is pointless and the righteous and wrongdoers would be treated as equals, contrary to divine wisdom.
rows.anchor: This is the premise which is substantiated from the oaths sworn in the previous verses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here saʿy means the consequences of effort, as shown by 53:39–40, rather than effort itself.
rows.anchor: used not only for effort it is also used for the consequences

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shattā is the plural of shatīt, meaning separate or different; human nature and reason require righteous and wrongful deeds to have different outcomes.
rows.anchor: requirement of human nature and intellect

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Judgment is necessary so good and evil receive different outcomes; without it, people could go free for all deeds, a notion the Qur’an challenges at 23:115 and 68:35–36.
rows.anchor: this world is nothing but a place of merrymaking

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about giving while God-fearing excludes boasting and worldly motives: the giver seeks God’s pleasure and fears the Day when deeds alone avail, as illustrated at 76:7–10.
rows.anchor: the purpose of this spending in the way of God should not be to boast and brag or some other worldly motive

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In al-ḥusnā, an omitted noun such as al-ʿāqibah (fate or outcome) is understood: the virtuous believe spending and goodness will bring good results.
rows.anchor: The implication is that they have faith that spending in the way of God and virtue will reap good results for them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fear of the Hereafter and belief in reward motivate virtue; without such faith, a person lacks an urge to give or gives for worldly benefit, without divine blessing, as 107:1–3 illustrates.
rows.anchor: will be rewarded in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-yusrā also suppresses a noun such as al-ʿāqibah; God helps the virtuous by removing obstacles and strengthening their desire to continue, as at 29:69.
rows.anchor: The Almighty facilitates a person who adopts the path of virtue by removing the hardships that come his way

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The destination is called al-yusrā because the reckoning is easy, as described at 84:7–8.
rows.anchor: his reckoning will be easy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who treat worldly life as ultimate are miserly, heedless of the Hereafter, and lack resolve for its reward; God lets them pursue their chosen way toward hardship.
rows.anchor: They are misers and callously guard their wealth and have no fear of the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God leaves people without courage for virtue to their base desires; they may seem to progress smoothly until death, then face the steep hardship of 74:17.
rows.anchor: they reach the end of their lives

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The virtuous fight their base desires at every step and grow stronger through that struggle, eventually reaching the servants’ company and Paradise described at 89:29–30.
rows.anchor: gradually gain the strength needed to fight

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā in verse 11 may be negative or interrogative; Islahi prefers the interrogative reading because it adds emphasis.
rows.anchor: an emphasis shall be added to the verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wealthy are warned that wealth benefits them permanently only when spent for God and preserved for eternal life; otherwise it becomes a source of doom.
rows.anchor: spending it for the cause of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s responsibility is to guide people through His Messenger, not force them to follow; accepting guidance is their responsibility, and their outcomes follow their choice.
rows.anchor: It is not His responsibility to force this guidance on people. Accepting this guidance is their responsibility.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both this world and the next are in God’s control; neither personal strategy nor racial status and deities can secure benefit, and everyone faces God alone, as discussed at 53:25.
rows.anchor: achieve anything in this world nor in the next.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wealthy may credit their riches to their own intelligence, like Qārūn’s claim at 28:78; Islahi says the verse overturns this self-reliant capitalist mentality because all gain comes from God.
rows.anchor: in the next is also from God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning addresses Quraysh: persistent deniers of truth face the blazing fire, while those who spend to attain purity are protected from it.
rows.anchor: people who spend their wealth to attain purity will be shielded from this fire.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrast is between rejecters of God’s Messengers and believers, not degrees of wickedness or piety; conclusive warning leaves Messenger-rejecters no legitimate excuse, making them the most wretched.
rows.anchor: less pious and the more pious
